questions.article: Aspiring for More and Settling for Less
questions.q: After studying people who live in frustration, what cause does the editorial identify?
options: Lack of education
Not quite. The article says: Unrealistic goals that can never be reached.
Too little ambition
Not quite. The article says: Unrealistic goals that can never be reached.
Unkind employers
Not quite. The article says: Unrealistic goals that can never be reached.
Unrealistic goals that can never be reached
Yes. The remedy: aspire for more, but be content with less.
questions.rationale: “There is no other reason for this, except that of having unrealistic goals.”

questions.article: Aspiring for More and Settling for Less
questions.q: Why does the editorial recall that Nehru first tried the law before entering public life?
options: To show that one should never change course
Not quite. The article says: To show that when one option fails, there are others – take the next and try again.
To show that when one option fails, there are others – take the next and try again
Right. “Don’t give up, plan once again.”
To show that law is a poor profession
Not quite. The article says: To show that when one option fails, there are others – take the next and try again.
To show that success comes from family name
Not quite. The article says: To show that when one option fails, there are others – take the next and try again.
questions.rationale: “In this world, there are always several options and if one option does not work, one should take another and try it out.”

questions.q: “Even a bullock cart will do better than a jet plane which has no sense of direction.” What principle is meant?
options: Machines cannot be trusted
Not quite. The article says: Direction matters more than speed – first make sure you are heading the right way.
Old methods are the best
Not quite. The article says: Direction matters more than speed – first make sure you are heading the right way.
Slow travel is safer
Not quite. The article says: Direction matters more than speed – first make sure you are heading the right way.
Direction matters more than speed – first make sure you are heading the right way
Well read. Motion alone gets nowhere worth going.
questions.rationale: “It is direction that is all important… Starting out in the right direction is the first important principle of success.”

questions.q: The article says success is reached by the ladder, not the lift. What does this mean?
options: Tall buildings should be avoided
Not quite. The article says: Progress comes step by step, paying the price at each stage; there are no buttons to press.
Only the young can succeed
Not quite. The article says: Progress comes step by step, paying the price at each stage; there are no buttons to press.
Progress comes step by step, paying the price at each stage; there are no buttons to press
Yes. One accepts loss before gain.
Help from others should be refused
Not quite. The article says: Progress comes step by step, paying the price at each stage; there are no buttons to press.
questions.rationale: “The climb is up the ladder one step after another, you cannot make a success of your life by the lift expecting it to do everything for you.”

questions.q: Why does the article compare the habit of suspicion to smoking?
options: It harms the person himself and also pollutes the atmosphere for everyone, destroying trust
Well reasoned. It is a social, not just a private, evil.
It is easily given up
Not quite. The article says: It harms the person himself and also pollutes the atmosphere for everyone, destroying trust.
It is expensive
Not quite. The article says: It harms the person himself and also pollutes the atmosphere for everyone, destroying trust.
It is found mostly among the old
Not quite. The article says: It harms the person himself and also pollutes the atmosphere for everyone, destroying trust.
questions.rationale: “The habit of suspicion is like smoking. It not only ruins the health of the individual who has this bad habit, but it also pollutes the whole of the social atmosphere.”

questions.q: Every day something we wanted fails to happen. How can such moments lead to God-realization, according to the article?
options: By teaching us to want nothing
Not quite. The article says: Each reminds us of our limits – and where man’s limit ends, God’s domain begins.
By making us try harder next time
Not quite. The article says: Each reminds us of our limits – and where man’s limit ends, God’s domain begins.
Each reminds us of our limits – and where man’s limit ends, God’s domain begins
Correct. Open to everyone, educated or not.
By showing us whom to blame
Not quite. The article says: Each reminds us of our limits – and where man’s limit ends, God’s domain begins.
questions.rationale: “Whenever man reaches his boundary, he should realize that immediately after this, the boundary of God starts.”

questions.q: What does the article say forgiveness awakens in the other person, where tit-for-tat arouses the ego?
options: Fear
Not quite. The article says: The conscience.
Pride
Not quite. The article says: The conscience.
Curiosity
Not quite. The article says: The conscience.
The conscience
Right. And conscience plays a positive role in disputes.
questions.rationale: “If you follow the tit-for-tat policy, it arouses the ego of the other person, whereas if you follow the policy of forgiveness, it will activate the other person’s conscience.”

questions.q: “If forgiveness is a full stop, revenge is punctuated by commas.” What is meant?
options: Forgiveness is brief; revenge takes planning
Not quite. The article says: Forgiveness ends an unwanted situation; revenge keeps extending it.
Forgiveness is final only in books
Not quite. The article says: Forgiveness ends an unwanted situation; revenge keeps extending it.
Forgiveness ends an unwanted situation; revenge keeps extending it
Yes. A chain of action and reaction.
Forgiveness is silent; revenge is spoken
Not quite. The article says: Forgiveness ends an unwanted situation; revenge keeps extending it.
questions.rationale: “Forgiveness means ending an unwanted situation, while taking revenge means endlessly extending it.”

questions.q: A Companion explained taqwa to Umar by asking how he walks a path with thorny bushes on both sides. What is the point of the image?
options: Living with caution and restraint – gathering oneself in so as not to be caught in life’s snares
Exactly. The path of avoidance, not entanglement.
Clearing every thorn before moving on
Not quite. The article says: Living with caution and restraint – gathering oneself in so as not to be caught in life’s snares.
Walking as fast as possible
Not quite. The article says: Living with caution and restraint – gathering oneself in so as not to be caught in life’s snares.
Staying at home to be safe
Not quite. The article says: Living with caution and restraint – gathering oneself in so as not to be caught in life’s snares.
questions.rationale: “Umar Farooq replied, ‘I gathered my clothes close to me and moved ahead cautiously’. The Companion said, ‘This is the meaning of taqwa.’”

questions.q: When, according to the article, is a funeral prayer truly meaningful?
options: When it is performed slowly
Not quite. The article says: When another’s death makes you remember and prepare for your own.
When it is followed by a meal
Not quite. The article says: When another’s death makes you remember and prepare for your own.
When another’s death makes you remember and prepare for your own
Well read. As if praying at your own funeral.
When it is attended by a great crowd
Not quite. The article says: When another’s death makes you remember and prepare for your own.
questions.rationale: “A truly meaningful funeral prayer is one in which someone else’s death provokes you to remember your own impending death.”
